query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A combined predictive approach that separately treats electronic transport via ab initio electronic structure and lattice transport via anharmonic phonon dynamics incorporating realistic oxygen defect scattering and nanoscale microstructural effects (grain boundaries) will predict the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr within ±20% of experimental measurements. In oxygen‐contaminated samples (≈1 wt.% O) over 300–1200 K, this method will show that the lattice contribution is reduced by approximately 30–40% relative to predictions from defect‐free models, while below 200 K the model will reveal that electronic and lattice contributions are of comparable magnitude.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy modeled as a chemically disordered BCC solid solution, initially represented as an ideal bulk crystal but then modified to include microstructural defects (grain boundaries) and 1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
generation.intervention: Apply a dual-module simulation framework that couples (i) an ab initio electronic structure calculation to predict electronic heat conductivity (κe) and (ii) an anharmonic atomistic phonon transport simulation (e.g., using advanced MD or self-consistent phonon methods) that explicitly incorporates oxygen impurity scattering and grain boundary effects to compute the lattice heat conductivity (κL)
generation.conditions: Temperature range: Low temperatures below 200 K (where electronic and lattice contributions are comparable) and high temperatures between 300 K and 1200 K (with oxygen-contaminated samples representing 1 wt.% O); sample conditions reflective of typical experimental microstructures rather than ideal, defect-free crystals.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical disorder enhanced by oxygen impurity sites and microstructural grain boundaries which increase phonon scattering and lower κL.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen impurities and grain boundaries disturb local force constants and bond anharmonicity, leading to enhanced phonon scattering; by decoupling this process from electronic contributions (modeled via ab initio methods unaffected by these lattice distortions), the framework allows independent quantification of κL, thereby better matching observed low total conductivities at high temperatures and comparable contributions at low temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures, the predicted total thermal conductivity (κ_total = κe + κL) will fall in the range of 10–17 W/(K·m) as observed experimentally, with κL reduced by roughly 30–40% compared to predictions from simulations assuming defect-free crystals; below 200 K the model will yield comparable values for κL and κe.
generation.baseline: Existing models based on perfect, defect-free bulk crystal simulations or analytical estimates using Debye temperatures that neglect oxygen and grain boundary effects tend to overestimate κL and do not correctly reflect the temperature dependence seen in experiments.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for refractory high-entropy alloys similar to HfNbTaTiZr with typical oxygen contamination (~1 wt.%) and microstructures exhibiting significant grain boundary density; it may require adjustment for alloys with very different defect or chemical order characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., PMC4735586::web::012::thermal_conductivity and the research query observations on low and high temperature behavior) have modeled phonon scattering in defect-free alloys, the quantitative impact of oxygen and grain boundary scattering on phonon lifetimes remains uncertain. New aspects in this study include explicitly simulating oxygen-induced force-constant fluctuations and realistic microstructures, which have not been directly combined in previous predictive efforts.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled oxygen levels (e.g., near 1 wt.% and with minimal oxygen) and characterized grain sizes. Measure the total thermal conductivity over two temperature regions: below 200 K and between 300 K to 1200 K. In parallel, perform separate ab initio electronic conductivity measurements (e.g., using terahertz spectroscopy or low-frequency electrical conductivity methods) and advanced phonon lifetime measurements (e.g., via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering) to independently determine κe and κL.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity (κ_total) via laser flash or similar techniques
Low-temperature electronic and lattice contributions separately (if possible via Wiedemann-Franz law and phonon spectroscopy)
Phonon linewidths and lifetimes to assess phonon scattering enhancements
Microstructure characterization (grain size, oxygen concentration via APT or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-module model yields predicted κL values that are not reduced by at least 30% relative to defect-free simulations, or if the decoupling of κe and κL does not result in comparable contributions below 200 K and a total conductivity deviating by more than ±20% from the 10–17 W/(K·m) range at high temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder.
